scenarios.title: Etcd Snapshot Before Upgrade
scenarios.situation: You're about to upgrade the control plane. Company policy requires a verified etcd backup first. The cluster is kubeadm-built with etcd running as a static pod.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct backup command?
evidence: etcd running as static pod; certs in /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/
choices: `ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key snapshot save /backup/etcd-snapshot.db` then `snapshot status` to verify
`kubectl get etcd -o yaml > backup.yaml`; etcd backs up through the API server
`etcdctl backup --data-dir /var/lib/etcd`; the v2 backup command handles v3 data
Copy `/var/lib/etcd` while etcd is running; file copies are crash-consistent
scenarios.why: The supported backup path is `etcdctl snapshot save` against the live member with the proper TLS certs (etcd only listens on TLS). Always verify with `snapshot status`. Copying the data dir of a running etcd risks corruption, the v2 `backup` subcommand is deprecated, and the API server has no etcd-backup resource.
scenarios.hint: etcd only talks TLS, and it must be asked politely while running. Which subcommand is designed for online backups?

scenarios.title: Restore Gone Wrong
scenarios.situation: After a bad etcd restore attempt, the API server won't start: `etcdserver: request timed out`. You restored the snapshot with `etcdctl snapshot restore` into a fresh data dir.
choices: The static pod manifest still mounts the old data dir — you must update `--data-dir` in the etcd manifest to the restored directory (and ensure the old dir is moved aside), then let the kubelet restart the pod
Snapshots must be restored with `--data-dir` pointing at the live dir while etcd runs
The API server needs `--etcd-servers` updated after every restore
Restore requires deleting all worker nodes first so they re-register
scenarios.why: `snapshot restore` writes a NEW data directory; it does not overwrite the live one. For a static-pod etcd, you then point the manifest's hostPath/`--data-dir` at the restored directory (moving the corrupted original aside) so the kubelet recreates the pod on the restored data. Skipping the manifest update leaves etcd serving the old, broken data dir.
scenarios.hint: The restore wrote to a new directory. Does anything actually point at that new directory yet?

scenarios.title: Which CNI, and Why It Matters
scenarios.situation: A cluster needs NetworkPolicies enforced, but pods on the current CNI plugin ignore them. The team is choosing between Flannel (current) and Calico or Cilium.
scenarios.prompt: What is the key decision factor?
evidence: NetworkPolicy objects created; traffic still allowed between all pods
choices: Flannel (VXLAN backend) does not implement NetworkPolicy enforcement — you need a CNI that does (Calico, Cilium, or Weave), so the choice hinges on policy enforcement plus the operational trade-offs (eBPF vs iptables, observability needs)
All CNIs enforce NetworkPolicy; the policies must be re-applied after switching
Flannel enforces policies only with `Backend: host-gw`; switch the backend type
NetworkPolicy requires a service mesh; no CNI choice fixes this
scenarios.why: NetworkPolicy is only as good as the CNI implementing it — the API objects are inert without enforcement in the dataplane. Flannel provides simple overlay networking without policy enforcement. Calico (iptables/eBPF) and Cilium (eBPF) both enforce policy; the choice then turns on performance characteristics, observability (Hubble), and operational familiarity.
scenarios.hint: The Policy objects exist but nothing changes. Who is supposed to read them and act?

scenarios.title: CRD Version Migration
scenarios.situation: Your operator's CRD `databases.example.com` serves `v1alpha1` (stored) and `v1beta1`. You want to move storage to `v1` and drop `v1alpha1`. Users have hundreds of existing objects.
scenarios.prompt: What is the safe migration sequence?
evidence: versions: [v1alpha1 (storage: true, served: true), v1beta1 (served: true)]
choices: Add `v1` as served with a conversion webhook/strategy, flip `storage: true` to `v1`, run `kubectl get databases -o yaml` round-trip (or the storage-version migrator) to rewrite all objects in the new version, verify, then remove `v1alpha1` from served versions
Delete the CRD and recreate it with only `v1`; the operator recreates the objects
Just flip `storage: true` to `v1`; etcd converts objects lazily on next read
Edit each object by hand to change its `apiVersion` to `v1`
scenarios.why: Changing the storage version only affects newly written objects — existing objects stay in the old version until rewritten, and dropping a served version while objects still reference it orphans them. The safe path: serve both, migrate storage, force a rewrite of every object (read-modify-write round trip migrates them), verify none remain in the old version, then remove it. Deleting the CRD deletes all instances.
scenarios.hint: Flipping the storage flag changes the future, not the past. What has to happen to the hundreds of existing objects?

scenarios.title: Skewed Upgrade Order
scenarios.situation: A junior admin upgraded worker kubelets to v1.30 while the control plane is still v1.28. Now `kubectl` shows nodes as `NotReady` with version skew warnings.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct recovery, given the Kubernetes version-skew policy?
evidence:
kube-apiserver: v1.28.x
kubelet on workers: v1.30.x
NotReady; kubelet logs: version skew errors
choices: Downgrade the kubelets back to v1.28 (supported skew: kubelet may be at most 2 minor versions older than apiserver, never newer), then perform the proper order: upgrade control plane first (one minor at a time), then workers
Upgrade the control plane straight to v1.30 to match the kubelets; forward jumps are fine
Delete the NotReady nodes and rejoin them; rejoining resets the version check
Edit the kubelet config to set `version: v1.28`; the version is just a label
scenarios.why: The skew policy is strict: kube-apiserver first, then kubelets — and kubelets must never be newer than the apiserver (they may lag by up to 2 minors). Newer kubelets can send API calls the older apiserver doesn't understand. Recovery is to downgrade kubelets to a supported version, then upgrade properly: control plane one minor at a time (1.28→1.29→1.30), then nodes.
scenarios.hint: Which component is allowed to be newer — the client of the API, or the server? What does the skew policy say?

scenarios.title: Kubeadm Upgrade Stalls
scenarios.situation: `kubeadm upgrade plan` shows v1.29.4 available, but `kubeadm upgrade apply v1.29.4` hangs at 'waiting for the kubelet to boot up the control plane'. The etcd static pod keeps crash-looping.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely blocker and the safe next step?
evidence: [upgrade] waiting for the kubelet to boot up the control plane as etcd-...
choices: Inspect why the new etcd pod fails (certs, data-dir, manifest rendering) with `crictl logs` — a common cause is an expired or mismatched etcd certificate after the manifest was regenerated; fix the underlying pod failure rather than re-running apply blindly
Run `kubeadm upgrade apply --force`; force skips the health checks that are hanging
Delete the etcd data dir; the upgrade will recreate it from the API server
Reboot all control-plane nodes simultaneously to clear the stuck state
scenarios.why: `kubeadm upgrade apply` is transactional-ish: it renders new static manifests and waits for healthy pods. If etcd won't start, the upgrade cannot proceed — forcing it or deleting data risks the cluster's state store. The disciplined move is to read the etcd container logs, fix the concrete failure (often cert paths or SANs in the regenerated manifest), and let the kubelet converge.
scenarios.hint: The upgrade is waiting on etcd. Instead of forcing past the wait, what would tell you why etcd won't start?

scenarios.title: Privileged by Default
scenarios.situation: A namespace runs third-party charts; one pod deployed with `privileged: true` and `hostPID: true`. No policy prevents the next one.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct admission control?
choices: Enforce the Pod Security Standards via the built-in PodSecurity admission plugin: label the namespace `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline` (or `restricted`), which rejects privileged/host-namespaces pods at admission
Add a validating webhook later; admission can wait
Tell chart authors not to use privileged; policy is social
Run everything in kube-system; policies don't apply there
scenarios.why: Pod Security Standards (privileged/baseline/restricted) enforced by the built-in PodSecurity admission controller are the standard, no-webhook path — namespace labels select the policy. kube-system exemptions are exactly why workloads shouldn't live there.
scenarios.hint: Which admission plugin enforces the built-in security profiles?

scenarios.title: The Tag That Moved
scenarios.situation: An incident traces to `image: web:stable` — but `stable` was repointed to a different build after deploy. Nobody can say which bits actually ran.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct image reference hygiene?
evidence: which digest ran during the incident window?
choices: Pin images by digest (`image: web@sha256:bbb...`) in production manifests — digests are immutable content addresses; tags are mutable pointers. Keep human-readable tags for humans, digests for the cluster
Use `imagePullPolicy: Always`; that freezes the image
Tags are fine; just don't repoint them
Delete old images from the registry; only one build can exist
scenarios.why: Tags mutate; digests don't. Incident forensics ('what ran at 2 AM?') is only answerable with immutable references. imagePullPolicy controls *when* the kubelet pulls, not *which* bits the tag points to.
scenarios.hint: Which reference can never silently change meaning?

scenarios.title: Flat Network, Loud Neighbor
scenarios.situation: A compromised frontend pod scanned the cluster network freely — every pod can reach every other pod on any port. There are no NetworkPolicies.
evidence: lateral movement via open pod network
choices: Default-deny ingress (and egress) NetworkPolicies per namespace, then explicit allow rules for required flows (frontend→api:443, api→db:5432) — least-privilege networking contains lateral movement
NetworkPolicies are only for ingress; egress can't be restricted
Encrypt everything with mTLS; encryption replaces segmentation
Put each tier in its own cluster; policies don't scale
scenarios.why: Kubernetes networking is flat by default — NetworkPolicy is the segmentation primitive. Default-deny both directions plus explicit allows implements zero-trust networking; mTLS gives confidentiality/identity but not reachability control.
scenarios.hint: What makes the pod network *not* flat?

scenarios.title: The Token in Every Pod
scenarios.situation: Every pod mounts a service-account token by default, including batch jobs that never talk to the API. A compromised job pod's token was used to list secrets cluster-wide.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct service-account hygiene?
evidence: default SA bound to a broad Role (legacy)
choices: Set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on pods/service accounts that don't need the API, scope each workload's own ServiceAccount with least-privilege RBAC, and never bind the `default` SA to broad roles
Tokens are required for pods to run; they can't be disabled
Delete all service accounts; the API works without them
Rotate tokens weekly; rotation fixes over-permission
scenarios.why: Auto-mounted tokens are ambient authority — any process in the pod can present them. Disabling automount where unneeded plus per-workload least-privilege RBAC shrinks the blast radius. Rotation doesn't fix excessive permission.
scenarios.hint: Which pods actually need to call the API server?

scenarios.title: Syscalls You Didn't Order
scenarios.situation: A container escape CVE targets a rarely-used syscall. The cluster runs containers with the default (unconfined) seccomp profile.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct runtime hardening?
choices: Apply restrictive seccomp profiles (`seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}`) and AppArmor/SELinux profiles to workloads — shrinking the allowed syscall surface contains kernel-exploit classes; audit with `strace`/profilers first to avoid breaking legit syscalls
Seccomp is only for privileged pods; regular pods don't need it
Update the kernel; profiles are redundant with patching
Run containers as root so seccomp doesn't block anything
scenarios.why: seccomp filters the syscalls a container may invoke — RuntimeDefault blocks ~44 dangerous-by-default calls while allowing normal operation. It's defense-in-depth alongside patching: the CVE still exists, but the exploit path is closed.
scenarios.hint: What stands between a container process and the kernel's syscall table?

scenarios.title: What's Inside the Image?
scenarios.situation: A base image pulled 6 months ago ships a critical OpenSSL CVE. Nothing in the pipeline would have caught it before deploy.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct supply-chain control?
evidence: build → push → deploy; no scanning step
CVE-2026-xxxxx in openssl 3.0.x, image built 6 months ago
choices: Scan images in the pipeline (Trivy/Grype) with fail-on-critical gates, rebuild base images on a cadence, and sign the resulting images (cosign) with admission verification — scan for known CVEs, sign for provenance
Scanning slows the pipeline; rely on the base image maintainer
Pin the OS package versions; pinning prevents CVEs
Signatures replace scanning; signed images have no CVEs
scenarios.why: Scanning finds known vulnerabilities in layers; signing (cosign/Sigstore) proves who built the image; admission controllers enforce both. Pinning freezes versions (including vulnerable ones) — it aids reproducibility, not security. The controls compose: scan + rebuild + sign + verify.
scenarios.hint: Which control finds the CVE, and which proves who built the image?

scenarios.title: The Advanced Kubernetes Administration Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Advanced Kubernetes Administration is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Advanced Kubernetes Administration?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Advanced Kubernetes Administration issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Advanced Kubernetes Administration is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Advanced Kubernetes Administration supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Advanced Kubernetes Administration failure in K8S Cka Exceed.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Advanced Kubernetes Administration
evidence: All Advanced Kubernetes Administration components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

lessons.title: Advanced Kubernetes Administration — Core concepts
concepts: etcd is the cluster's state store: back it up with `etcdctl snapshot save` over TLS before any control-plane change, and verify with `snapshot status`. Restore writes a new data dir — the static pod manifest must be repointed at it.
The CNI plugin owns the pod network dataplane. NetworkPolicy objects are inert unless the CNI enforces them — Flannel doesn't; Calico and Cilium do (with different eBPF/iptables trade-offs).

CRDs are versioned APIs you define. Storage version migration is a sequence: serve both versions, flip storage, rewrite every object (round-trip), verify, then drop the old version — deleting the CRD deletes all its instances.
Version skew policy: upgrade the control plane first, one minor at a time; kubelets may lag up to two minors behind the apiserver but must never be newer.

`kubeadm upgrade` renders new static-pod manifests and waits for healthy pods. When it stalls, read the failing component's container logs (often cert paths in the regenerated manifest) — never force past a broken etcd.

example.code:
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /backup/etcd-$(date +%F).db
etcdctl snapshot status /backup/etcd-$(date +%F).db
example.walkthrough: The pre-upgrade backup ritual: snapshot over TLS with the etcd PKI certs, then verify the snapshot file is readable. An unverified backup is not a backup.

pitfalls: Common trap: copying /var/lib/etcd from a running member — use snapshot save instead.
Common trap: flipping a CRD storage version and assuming existing objects convert — they don't until rewritten.
Common trap: upgrading kubelets before the apiserver — skew policy forbids newer kubelets.

labs.title: Etcd Snapshot and Restore Drill
labs.objective: Take a verified etcd snapshot, simulate data loss, and restore the cluster from the snapshot.
steps: Snapshot: run `etcdctl snapshot save` with the etcd PKI certs against https://127.0.0.1:2379.
Verify with `etcdctl snapshot status` and record the hash and revision.
Create a canary ConfigMap, then simulate loss (in the drill environment, stop etcd / restore scenario per lab guide).
Restore with `etcdctl snapshot restore --data-dir` to a new directory and repoint the etcd static-pod manifest.
Confirm the API server is healthy and the canary ConfigMap is back: `kubectl get cm canary`.

checks.hint: Verify the snapshot file reports a hash.
After restore, the canary ConfigMap should exist again.

labs.title: Kubeadm Minor Upgrade, By the Book
labs.objective: Upgrade a kubeadm control plane one minor version following the supported order: etcd backup, control plane, then kubelets.
steps: Pre-flight: snapshot etcd and run `kubeadm upgrade plan` to confirm the target version path.
Upgrade kubeadm itself on the control-plane node (`apt-mark unhold` / install target version / hold).
Run `kubeadm upgrade apply vX.Y.Z` and wait for static pods to converge; check `kubectl get nodes` versions.
Upgrade kubelet + kubectl on the control-plane node, restart kubelet, confirm Ready.
Repeat the kubelet upgrade on each worker (drain, upgrade, uncordon) — never before the control plane is done.

checks.hint: The plan should show the upgrade path.
Nodes should report the new version after upgrade.

simulations.title: etcd before the upgrade
simulations.brief: The cluster is one minor behind and the upgrade window opens Saturday. The runbook's first step is the etcd backup — but the last backup is 4 months old and nobody has tested a restore. Work the pre-upgrade.

steps.symptom: Upgrade planned Saturday. Last etcd snapshot: 4 months ago. Restore tested: never.
evidence: etcd snapshots: 2026-06-01 (4 months ago). Location: control-plane disk (same disk as etcd).
Step 1: 'Back up etcd.' Step 2: 'Upgrade.' No verification step.
options: Take a fresh snapshot with etcdctl snapshot save over TLS, verify it with snapshot status, and copy it off the control-plane disk
The 4-month-old snapshot is fine — etcd barely changes
Skip the backup — the upgrade is routine
Back up after the upgrade to capture the new state
steps.explain: etcd is the cluster's state store: back it up with etcdctl snapshot save over TLS before any control-plane change, verify with snapshot status, and store it off the machine. A snapshot on the same disk as etcd protects against nothing.

steps.symptom: The snapshot is taken. Now prove it's usable before Saturday.
evidence: snapshot.db: 84MB, created today. snapshot status: OK.
Last restore rehearsal: never. Team: 'We've never needed one.'
options: Rehearse the restore on an isolated host: it writes a new data dir and the static pod manifest must be repointed at it
The snapshot status said OK — that's proof enough
Rehearsals risk breaking the test host — skip it
Restore directly on the production control plane to be sure
steps.explain: An untested backup is a hope, not a backup. Restore rehearsal teaches the real procedure: restore writes a new data directory, and the etcd static pod manifest must be repointed at it — a step you do not want to learn during an incident.

steps.symptom: Saturday arrives. Mid-upgrade, kubeadm stalls at the etcd health check.
evidence: kubeadm upgrade: 'waiting for etcd to become healthy' — 25 minutes.
options: Stop: read the etcd container logs, diagnose the health failure, and never force past a broken etcd
Force past it — the upgrade window is closing
Restart the whole control plane and try again
The health check is flaky — ignore it
steps.explain: When kubeadm stalls, read the failing component's container logs — often cert paths in the regenerated manifest — and never force past a broken etcd. Forcing an upgrade over an unhealthy state store turns a stall into data loss.

simulations.debrief: etcd discipline: snapshot over TLS before control-plane changes, verify the snapshot, rehearse the restore (new data dir, repoint the manifest), and never force an upgrade past an unhealthy etcd.

simulations.title: The policy that did nothing
simulations.brief: The security team deployed NetworkPolicies to isolate the payments namespace. A penetration test walks straight through them. The YAML is valid and applied. Diagnose the dataplane.

steps.symptom: NetworkPolicy applied and valid, but traffic flows freely between namespaces. Pentest: full lateral movement.
evidence: apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1, kind: NetworkPolicy — valid, applied, endpoints selected.
CNI plugin: flannel. NetworkPolicy enforcement: not supported.
options: The CNI doesn't enforce NetworkPolicy — Flannel ignores them; the policy objects are inert without an enforcing dataplane
The YAML must have a typo — reapply it
NetworkPolicies take 24 hours to take effect — wait
Delete and recreate the policies with different names
steps.explain: NetworkPolicy objects are inert unless the CNI enforces them — Flannel doesn't; Calico and Cilium do, with different eBPF/iptables trade-offs. The API accepted the objects because they're valid; the dataplane ignored them because it can't enforce them.

steps.symptom: The fix is a CNI migration to an enforcing plugin. The team wants to do it Friday afternoon.
evidence: CNI swap: Friday 16:00, all nodes, no rollback plan. 'It's just networking.'
CNI swap restarts the pod network dataplane on every node.
options: Schedule the migration in a window with a node-by-node plan and a tested rollback — the dataplane restart affects every pod
Friday afternoon is fine — networking changes are low-risk
Do it without a rollback plan to keep it simple
Migrate the CNI on production first to prove it works
steps.explain: The CNI owns the pod network dataplane: swapping it restarts networking on every node. That deserves a maintenance window, a node-by-node rollout, and a rollback plan — 'just networking' is how you learn what the dataplane actually does.

steps.symptom: After migration, one legacy app breaks — it relied on unrestricted pod traffic.
evidence: Legacy monitor: scrapes metrics from every namespace. Assumed flat network.
Default posture after migration: deny-all between namespaces (as designed).
options: Write explicit allow policies for the monitor's legitimate traffic — the breakage is the policy working, and exceptions must be declared
Remove the deny-all — the legacy app is more important
Give the monitor host-network access instead
Exempt the legacy app from all policies permanently
steps.explain: Deny-by-default working as designed will break things that depended on the flat network — that's the migration surfacing implicit trust. The fix is explicit allow policies for legitimate flows, not dismantling the posture for one app.

simulations.debrief: Know your CNI: policy objects without dataplane enforcement are decoration. Migrate deliberately, expect implicit-trust breakage, and encode the legitimate exceptions as explicit policy.

simulations.title: CRD version migration
simulations.brief: The platform's custom Database CRD needs to move its storage version from v1alpha1 to v1. There are 400 instances in production. One wrong step deletes them all. Sequence the migration.

steps.symptom: CRD serves v1alpha1 (storage). v1 is added to the schema. 400 instances exist. The team wants to 'just flip storage to v1'.
evidence: versions: [v1alpha1 (storage: true), v1 (storage: false, served: true)]. instances: 400.
'Flip storage to v1 and delete v1alpha1 — one change.'
options: Follow the sequence: serve both, flip storage, rewrite every object (round-trip), verify, then drop the old version
Flip storage and delete v1alpha1 in one change — it's atomic
Delete the CRD and recreate it at v1 — clean slate
Storage version doesn't matter — it's metadata
steps.explain: CRD storage migration is a sequence: serve both versions, flip the storage version, rewrite every object so it's actually stored at v1 (round-trip), verify, then remove v1alpha1. Skipping the rewrite leaves objects stored in a version you then delete.

steps.symptom: Storage flipped to v1, but the rewrite job was skipped — 'the flip is what matters.'
evidence: Sample of 50 objects: 47 still serialized as v1alpha1.
Next step: remove v1alpha1 from the CRD.
options: Stop: run the round-trip rewrite first — removing v1alpha1 while objects are still stored as v1alpha1 destroys them
Proceed — the storage flip converted everything automatically
The 47 are probably test objects
Rewrite is optional — the API converts on read
steps.explain: Flipping the storage version changes where new writes go; existing objects stay serialized in the old version until rewritten. Deleting the CRD version — or the CRD itself — deletes all its instances. The rewrite is the step that makes the migration real.

steps.symptom: Migration complete and verified. The old version lingers 'just in case'.
evidence: versions: [v1alpha1 (served: true), v1 (storage: true)]. All 400 objects verified at v1.
v1alpha1 served 'temporarily' — 8 months ago in a similar migration.
options: Drop v1alpha1 now that verification is complete — lingering versions are debt that the next migration trips over
Keep it forever — serving two versions is harmless
Keep it until someone complains
Drop it without verification to save time
steps.explain: The sequence ends with dropping the old version after verification. 'Temporary' served versions become permanent API surface that every future migration must carry — finish the sequence.

simulations.debrief: CRD version migration: serve both, flip storage, round-trip rewrite every object, verify, drop the old version. Deleting the CRD deletes all its instances — there are no shortcuts in this sequence.

simulations.title: kubelet newer than apiserver
simulations.brief: A node was 'upgraded' to kubelet 1.31 while the apiserver runs 1.29. The node is NotReady and the engineer insists newer-is-better. Explain the skew policy.

steps.symptom: Node NotReady after its kubelet was upgraded past the apiserver version.
evidence: apiserver: v1.29. kubelet: v1.31. Node status: NotReady.
'Newer is better — the kubelet should be ahead.'
options: The skew policy forbids it: kubelets may lag up to two minors behind the apiserver but must never be newer
Newer kubelets are fine — the NotReady is a coincidence
Upgrade the apiserver to 1.31 immediately to match
Restart the kubelet — version mismatches fix themselves
steps.explain: Version skew policy: upgrade the control plane first, one minor at a time; kubelets may lag up to two minors behind the apiserver but must never be newer. A newer kubelet can send API calls the older apiserver doesn't understand.

steps.symptom: The approved path: bring the cluster to 1.30, then 1.31, control plane first each time.
evidence: Step 1: apiserver 1.29 -> 1.30. Step 2: kubelets -> 1.30. Step 3: repeat for 1.31.
Proposal: 'Jump the apiserver straight to 1.31 — one outage instead of two.'
options: One minor at a time: the skew policy and upgrade tooling are validated for single-minor steps, not jumps
Jump to 1.31 — fewer maintenance windows is better
Skip 1.30 for the apiserver but do it for kubelets
Versions are just numbers — jump freely
steps.explain: Upgrade the control plane first, one minor at a time. Multi-minor jumps skip the migration steps each minor performs — etcd schema, API conversions, component contracts — and land you in untested territory.

steps.symptom: During the 1.30 upgrade, a teammate upgrades a kubelet to 1.31 'to get ahead'.
evidence: One kubelet at 1.31 against apiserver 1.30. Status: NotReady, again.
Second occurrence of the same violation this month.
options: Drain, downgrade the kubelet to the supported skew, and put the skew rule in the upgrade runbook so it stops recurring
Leave it — one node at 1.31 is harmless
Upgrade everything to 1.31 right now to match the node
Cordon the node and forget it
steps.explain: Fix the node (drain, downgrade into supported skew) and fix the process (the skew rule goes in the runbook). Recurring violations are a process failure wearing an incident costume.

simulations.debrief: Skew policy is a hard rule, not guidance: control plane first, one minor at a time, kubelets never newer than the apiserver. Put it in the runbook and the violations stop.

simulations.title: Upgrade stalled at etcd
simulations.brief: kubeadm upgrade has been 'waiting for the control plane' for 40 minutes. The window closes in 20. The loudest voice says force it. Work the stall.

steps.symptom: kubeadm upgrade preflight hangs: new apiserver static pod won't become healthy.
evidence: 'waiting for the kubelet to boot up the control plane as etcd... ' 40 minutes.
apiserver container: 'error loading cert: /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver-etcd-client.crt: no such file'.
options: The regenerated manifest points at a cert path that doesn't exist — fix the cert path issue, don't force the upgrade
Force the upgrade — the cert error is probably transient
Delete the static pod manifests and let them regenerate
Reboot the control-plane node
steps.explain: When kubeadm upgrade stalls, read the failing component's container logs — here, cert paths in the regenerated manifest. The stall is the tool refusing to proceed on a broken component; forcing past it deploys the brokenness.

steps.symptom: Cert path fixed, apiserver healthy. Now etcd reports a quorum warning on one member.
evidence: Member 3: 'took too long to apply' warnings, disk latency spikes.
options: Pause and resolve the etcd health issue first — never upgrade over an unhealthy state store
etcd always catches up — continue the upgrade
Remove the slow member and upgrade with two
The warnings are informational — proceed
steps.explain: Never force past a broken etcd: the state store's health is the precondition for everything above it. A member with disk-latency warnings during an upgrade is how you get a quorum loss mid-migration.

steps.symptom: Upgrade complete. The team wants to delete the pre-upgrade etcd snapshot 'to save disk'.
evidence: Retention policy: keep pre-upgrade snapshots 30 days.
options: Keep the snapshot per the retention policy — the upgrade isn't proven until the cluster has baked, and 84MB is cheap insurance
Delete it — the upgrade succeeded
Delete it — disk space is precious
Move it to the same disk as etcd for safekeeping
steps.explain: The pre-upgrade snapshot is rollback insurance with a 30-day retention for a reason: upgrade regressions surface over days, not minutes. Deleting the parachute because the jump looked fine is premature.

simulations.debrief: Stalled upgrades are diagnosed, not forced: read the component logs, fix cert paths, demand a healthy etcd before proceeding — and keep the pre-upgrade snapshot until the new version has proven itself.

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.
